name: Shangri-La diet

lead: The Shangri-La diet is a weight-loss approach created by psychologist Seth Roberts. It proposes that the body has a "set point" weight and that consuming a small amount of flavorless calories, such as light olive oil or sugar water, between meals lowers that set point and reduces appetite. A lower body-fat level shows up as a leaner face and physique.
Roberts published the idea in a 2006 book, which became a bestseller. Support comes largely from his self-experiments and animal research; critics have noted the lack of peer-reviewed human trials.

paras: Practitioners take a modest amount of bland calories (oil or unflavored sugar water) at spaced times away from flavored food, and track their appetite and weight over weeks. Some lifters in forums mention it as a way to stay lean.

Nutritionist David Jenkins called it cheap and safe while noting the lack of validating research. Added calories could matter for people with medical conditions, and anyone with a health condition would usually check with a clinician.

angle.text: Followers use it to reduce appetite and body fat, which lets facial structure and muscle show more clearly. The mechanism rests on Roberts' set-point theory.

lead: The Shangri-La diet is a weight-loss method and 2006 book by psychologist Seth Roberts.[1] It is used to reduce body fat, which makes the face look leaner and the physique more defined.

Roberts proposed a "set point", the weight the brain defends: appetite rises below it and falls above it. In his theory, flavorful calorie-dense foods raise the set point and flavorless calories lower it.[1] The method involves small amounts of flavorless calories, such as extra-light olive oil or unflavored sugar water, between meals, kept apart from flavored food.[1] Roberts reported about a pound of weight loss per week.[1]
The book reached the New York Times bestseller list in May 2006, largely through word of mouth.[1] A Hacker News discussion later covered the rise and fall of Roberts and the diet.[2]
infobox: Flavorless calories lower the set point

paras: Roberts drew on Pavlovian associative learning, a report on saccharin and rat growth, and his own observations on a 2000 trip to Paris.[1] He wrote that flavor-calorie associations raise the body's set point, while bland calories do not.[1]

UCLA medical professor John Ford criticized the lack of peer review; nutritionist David Jenkins also noted the lack of validating research but called it cheap and safe.[1] Roberts replied that there was no need for a big study to demonstrate the obvious.[1]

A T Nation lifter's thread links to a blog post in which an over-50 lifter says the diet still works for him two and a half years on.[3] Others discuss artificial sweeteners and related fat-loss frameworks nearby.[4]
No studies found. The theory draws on animal and conditioning research, and the book's evidence rests mostly on Roberts' self-experimentation.[1]
